title: SINKO v. THE SLOVAK REPUBLIC
summary:
In Sinko v. the Slovak Republic, the applicant, Mr. Sinko, a Slovak national and fireman residing in Trnava, brought a case against Slovakia after receiving a death threat. The threat, signed "Gypsies from Trnava," followed his public opposition at a local meeting to the accommodation of persons of Roma origin in his neighborhood. Although the applicant himself is not described as Roma or Traveller, the case arose from tensions surrounding Roma settlement in Trnava.

The harm at the center of the case was the applicant’s exposure to threats and distress after his photograph was published in a weekly newspaper, linking him to anti-Roma sentiment. Mr. Sinko sought compensation from the publisher, claiming the publication endangered his safety and disrupted his family life. However, his civil claim was discontinued because he could not pay the required court fees, and his requests for exemption were denied by the Slovak courts, which found his income insufficiently low to justify exemption.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 § 1 (right of access to a court) and Article 8 (right to respect for private life) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Commission found the application inadmissible, concluding that the court fees were not excessive or disproportionate and that the Slovak courts had not acted arbitrarily. The Commission also found no unreasonable delay in the proceedings. The case is notable for illustrating the procedural barriers individuals may face in seeking remedies for threats linked to Roma-related community tensions, even when the applicant is not a member of the Roma or Traveller communities.
